claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has moderate hardness and strength but favorable ductility in its homogenized simple solid-solution state.
The simple solid-solution state of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi lacks fine-scale secondary precipitate or transformation-induced phases.
The absence of fine-scale secondary phases causes deformation in CoCrFeNiTi to be dominated by relatively unimpeded dislocation glide.
Relatively unimpeded dislocation glide keeps the hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi low while preserving plasticity.
A minor Al addition followed by annealing can stimulate nanoscale phase separation or ordering in CoCrFeNiTi.
Nanoscale precipitates or ordered domains pin dislocations.
Introducing nanoscale inhomogeneities creates additional barriers to dislocation glide.
Additional nanoscale barriers should increase the hardness and compressive strength of modified CoCrFeNiTi.
Precipitate- or ordering-induced strengthening may reduce the plasticity of modified CoCrFeNiTi.
Samples containing induced nanoscale precipitates should have measurably higher hardness and compressive strength than the starting equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
The increase in hardness and strength should be accompanied by reduced plasticity.
Transformation-induced effects in related HEAs are consistent with the predicted mechanical-property changes.
Alloy chemistry-induced phase stability has been associated with inherently higher strength in metastable dual-phase HEAs.
Annealing can produce a high hardness-modulus combination in at least one related Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Cu HEA.
The proposed mechanism is limited to equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloys at room temperature under quasi-static deformation.
The mechanism may not generalize to high-temperature or high-strain-rate deformation.
The kinetics of precipitate formation and the quantitative effect on CoCrFeNiTi mechanical properties are uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant increase in both hardness and compressive strength is proposed as a falsifying result.
Failure to detect precipitates or ordered phases after the intervention is proposed as falsification of the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The starting state is variously called homogenized, as-cast, and 'as-cast, fully homogenized.' As-cast and post-casting homogenized conditions are distinct processing states unless the processing sequence is explicitly clarified.

The hypothesis acknowledges that precipitate-formation kinetics are uncertain, yet treats failure to form or detect precipitates as falsification. That outcome would primarily show failure of the intervention to create the mediator, not disprove the proposed strengthening mechanism.
